items.text: What is the core holding of Rory v Continental Insurance Co on how Michigan courts read insurance policies?
Unambiguous contracts, including insurance policies, are enforced as written unless a provision violates law or public policy. Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
Can a Michigan court refuse to enforce a clear insurance-policy provision because the court thinks it is unreasonable?
No. Rory holds that judicial determinations of "reasonableness" are an invalid basis to refuse to enforce unambiguous contractual provisions. Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
Does Michigan recognize the reasonable-expectations doctrine in insurance disputes?
No. Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003), held the rule of reasonable expectations has no application in Michigan and overruled the cases that had recognized it.

A homeowner believes their policy "should" cover a loss because that is what they always assumed homeowners insurance covers, even though the written exclusion is unambiguous. What doctrine, if any, saves the claim?

None. Under Wilkie, an insured's subjective or reasonable expectation cannot override unambiguous policy language. The only paths back into coverage are showing genuine ambiguity or a recognized contract defense.
Under Klapp v United Insurance Group Agency, when is an insurance contract ambiguous?

When its provisions are capable of conflicting interpretations; if two provisions of the same contract irreconcilably conflict, the language is ambiguous. Klapp v United Ins Group Agency, Inc, 468 Mich 459 (2003).
Where does contra proferentem fit in the sequence of contract interpretation under Klapp?
Last. Klapp treats contra proferentem as a tie-breaker used only after all conventional interpretation methods, including relevant extrinsic evidence, have been applied and found wanting.
TRAP: What is the correct official reporter citation for Klapp v United Insurance Group Agency?
468 Mich 459 (2003), not 468 Mich 416. The 459 page cite was confirmed against the official reporter.

A homeowner's policy's declarations page and an endorsement define "flood" two different, conflicting ways. The insured wants the ambiguity resolved against the carrier immediately. Is that the right next step under Klapp?

No. Under Klapp, once the language is ambiguous its meaning is a question of fact, and the factfinder (a jury, in Klapp itself) first considers relevant extrinsic evidence of what the parties actually intended. Only if intent still cannot be determined does contra proferentem apply against the drafter. Klapp v United Ins Group Agency, Inc, 468 Mich 459 (2003).
Under Heniser v Frankenmuth Mutual, who has the burden of proving a loss falls within the coverage grant?
The insured. Heniser v Frankenmuth Mut Ins Co, 449 Mich 155 (1995), holds it is the insured's burden to establish that the claim falls within the terms of the policy.
Once an insured shows a loss falls within the coverage grant, who has the burden of proving an exclusion takes it back out?

The insurer. Heniser v Frankenmuth Mut Ins Co, 449 Mich 155 (1995), supplies the two step order and the insured's half of it. The insurer's half is stated in Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014), quoting Fresard v Mich Millers Mut Ins Co, 414 Mich 686, 694 (1982): the insurer should bear the burden of proving an absence of coverage. Heniser itself never says the insurer carries that burden.

A carrier denies a wind-damage claim citing a wear-and-tear exclusion. The homeowner already showed the roof damage fits the wind peril. Who must now prove the wear-and-tear exclusion actually applies?

The insurer. Heniser sets the two step order and holds the insured must first show the claim falls within the terms of the policy. Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014), quoting Fresard, 414 Mich 686, 694 (1982), puts the burden of proving an absence of coverage, including an exclusion, on the insurer.
TRAP: Does Heniser tell you who must prove that an EXCEPTION to an exclusion (for example, an ensuing-loss carve-out) applies?

No. Heniser states the two step order (coverage first, then exclusion) and the insured's burden to establish that the claim falls within the terms of the policy. The insurer's burden on exclusions comes from Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014), not from Heniser. Neither opinion discusses exceptions to exclusions. Do not cite Heniser, or any Michigan case you have not opened, for the exception burden.
What does Kirschner v Process Design say about using waiver or estoppel to broaden insurance coverage?

Usually, waiver and estoppel will not be applied to broaden coverage to protect against risks not included in, or expressly excluded from, the policy. Kirschner v Process Design Assocs, 459 Mich 587 (1999).
Why does Kirschner say waiver/estoppel usually cannot broaden coverage?
Because an insurance company should not be required to pay for a loss for which it has charged no premium.
What two situations does Kirschner acknowledge in which courts have extended coverage through waiver or estoppel, and on what condition?

(1) The insurer misrepresented the terms of the policy to the insured, or (2) the insurer defended the insured without reserving the right to deny coverage, and only when the inequity to the insurer from broadened coverage is outweighed by the inequity suffered by the insured. Kirschner describes these as what courts have done 'in some instances'; it applied neither. Kirschner v Process Design Assocs, 459 Mich 587 (1999).
An adjuster verbally tells a homeowner "don't worry, we'll cover the detached garage," but the policy has no endorsement for it. Does that verbal statement create coverage under Kirschner?

Almost never. A bare verbal assurance is not one of the situations Kirschner describes (misrepresentation of the policy's terms, or defending the insured without a reservation of rights), and even those require the inequity to the insured to outweigh the inequity to the insurer. Get every coverage commitment in writing. Kirschner v Process Design Assocs, 459 Mich 587 (1999).
In Salesin v State Farm, did self-performing the repairs (not hiring a general contractor) defeat the insured's claim for overhead and profit?
No. The court held that not actually incurring GC overhead and profit costs is "not dispositive." Salesin v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 229 Mich App 346 (1998).
What test did Salesin adopt from the Pennsylvania Gilderman case for including O&P in an ACV payment?

Repair or replacement costs include any cost an insured is "reasonably likely to incur" in repairing or replacing a covered loss, which in some instances includes a general contractor's overhead and profit.
TRAP: Does Salesin establish that O&P must always and automatically be included in every ACV payment?
No. Salesin expressly says Gilderman does not support the position that O&P should always and automatically be included. The test is "reasonably likely to incur," not an automatic rule.
A homeowner self-performs a multi-trade rebuild (roof, drywall, flooring, paint) after a covered loss. Is O&P reasonably owed on the ACV payment under Salesin's adopted test?

This is the strongest fact pattern under the adopted test. A homeowner coordinating several trades in sequence is the situation Gilderman describes as reasonably likely to need a general contractor, and Salesin holds that not actually hiring one is 'not dispositive.' It is still an application of the 'reasonably likely to incur' test, not an automatic rule. Salesin v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 229 Mich App 346 (1998).
A homeowner self-performs a single-trade repair (carpet replacement only). Is O&P as strong a claim under Salesin's test?
No. A single trade job does not typically require coordinating a general contractor, so it is a weaker argument that O&P is "reasonably likely to incur" than a multi-trade rebuild.
What Michigan case is the controlling authority on whether anti-concurrent-causation (ACC) clauses are enforced?
Sunshine Motors, Inc v New Hampshire Ins Co, 209 Mich App 58 (1995), a published Michigan Court of Appeals opinion.
In Sunshine Motors, heavy rain and a wood-blocked drain both contributed to flooding at a dealership. What did the exclusion's ACC preamble say, and how did the court rule?

The exclusion applied "regardless of any other cause or event that contributes concurrently or in any sequence to the loss." The court held the policy expressly excluded coverage no matter whether the blocked drain was a direct, indirect, principal, or merely contributing cause.
Has the Michigan Supreme Court adopted the 'concurrent causation' (dual causation) theory to override an unambiguous policy exclusion?

No. In Vanguard Ins Co v Clarke, 438 Mich 463 (1991), the Court reversed a Court of Appeals panel that had applied the 'minority rule' of concurrent causation, holding it saw no basis for that doctrine to 'nullify an unambiguous insurance policy exclusion' (an auto exclusion in a homeowner's liability policy). No Michigan Supreme Court first-party property case adopting the doctrine was opened. Vanguard Ins Co v Clarke, 438 Mich 463 (1991).

A basement floods from a combination of sump-pump failure (potentially covered) and surface water (excluded, with ACC language in that specific exclusion). Under Sunshine Motors, can the carrier deny the whole loss?

Yes, if the ACC language is actually in the surface-water exclusion. Under Sunshine Motors it does not matter whether the sump failure was the principal factor or merely a contributing factor; the exclusion applies. Sunshine Motors says nothing about carving out damage caused solely by the covered peril; any such argument rests on the exclusion's own 'caused by' wording, not on a Michigan holding. Sunshine Motors, Inc v New Hampshire Ins Co, 209 Mich App 58 (1995).
What is the Michigan Court of Appeals's key holding in Gavrilides Management Co v Michigan Insurance Co on "direct physical loss"?

The pandemic executive orders did not result in 'direct physical loss of or damage to property.' The word 'physical' requires the loss or damage to have 'some manner of tangible and measurable presence or effect in, on, or to the premises,' and the restaurants were 'closed by impersonal operation of a general law, not because anything about or inside the particular premises at issue had physically changed.' Gavrilides Mgmt Co v Michigan Ins Co, COA No. 354418, published Feb 1, 2022.
A restaurant owner claims civil-authority business-income coverage because a government order closed indoor dining, with no physical damage to the building. Does Gavrilides support that claim?

No. Gavrilides held the orders did not cause direct physical loss: 'physical' requires a tangible and measurable presence or effect on the premises, and closure by operation of a general law is not a physical change to the property. The court also held the civil-authority provision was not satisfied and, separately, that the policy's virus exclusion applied. Gavrilides Mgmt Co v Michigan Ins Co, COA No. 354418 (2022).
What is the publication status and docket number of Gavrilides Management Co v Michigan Insurance Co?
Published, Michigan Court of Appeals No. 354418, decided February 1, 2022.
What does MCL 500.2833(1)(a) require every Michigan fire insurance policy to provide, at minimum?

Coverage for the actual cash value (ACV) of the property at the time of the loss, subject to the policy's other provisions. This is a statutory floor, not itself a definition of how ACV is calculated.
How does DIFS Bulletin 2024-26-INS describe what ACV is "ordinarily understood to mean"?

The loss of value due to wear and tear, deterioration, and obsolescence to physical or tangible items. Nontangible items such as labor are not physical objects and do not deteriorate, age, or decline in value.
What is the difference between actual cash value (ACV) and replacement cost value (RCV) on a Michigan homeowners policy?

ACV, as the Gilderman definition adopted in Salesin puts it, means 'repair or replacement cost less depreciation.' A replacement-cost policy pays more, but usually only after the work is done: the State Farm policy in Salesin paid 'the actual cash value of the damage' until actual repair or replacement was completed, then any additional replacement-cost payment, limited to what the insured actually and necessarily spent, on a claim made within 180 days of the loss. The gap is what claims people call recoverable depreciation. Salesin v State Farm Fire & Cas Co, 229 Mich App 346 (1998).
What four items does DIFS Bulletin 2024-26-INS define as "nontangible items"?
Labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit.
For which policies, and starting when, does Bulletin 2024-26-INS require a standalone optional endorsement to depreciate nontangible items?
Personal-lines homeowners or dwelling policies issued or renewed effective July 1, 2025 or after. The bulletin does not address commercial lines.
Besides being a standalone endorsement, what two other conditions does Bulletin 2024-26-INS place on a nontangible-item depreciation endorsement?
It must be an optional coverage, and because it reduces coverage, it must be offered for a commensurate reduction in premium.
TRAP: Does Bulletin 2024-26-INS ban insurers from depreciating labor, taxes, fees, or overhead and profit?
No. It does not ban the practice. It conditions it on a standalone, optional, premium-reduced endorsement for personal-lines HO/DP policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025.
What Michigan statute does DIFS cite as the basis for Bulletin 2024-26-INS's transparency requirement?

MCL 500.2236(5), which bars policy forms from containing inconsistent, ambiguous, or misleading clauses, or exceptions and conditions that unreasonably or deceptively affect the risk purported to be assumed.
Is a DIFS bulletin the same as a statute in terms of legal force?

No. A bulletin is interpretive/regulatory guidance, not an act of the legislature. DIFS superseded the prior Bulletin 2024-18-INS with Bulletin 2024-26-INS through the same administrative process, without any legislative vote.

A Michigan homeowners policy renews on August 1, 2025 and the insurer wants to depreciate labor and O&P in the definition section of the policy form itself, without an endorsement. Is that compliant with Bulletin 2024-26-INS?
No. Because the renewal is after July 1, 2025, the insurer must use a standalone optional endorsement, not a definition buried in the policy form, to depreciate nontangible items.
Which Michigan Supreme Court case states that the insurer bears the burden of proving an absence of coverage, such as an exclusion?

Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014). It restates Heniser's two step test, then quotes Fresard v Mich Millers Mut Ins Co, 414 Mich 686, 694 (1982): "[t]he insurer should bear the burden of proving an absence of coverage." The same passage adds that exclusionary clauses are strictly construed in favor of the insured, but that clear and specific exclusions must be enforced.
Rory says courts cannot police an insurance policy for reasonableness. Who does Michigan law assign that job to instead?

The state insurance regulator, through policy form approval. Rory points to MCL 500.2236, under which basic policy forms must be filed with and approved by the Commissioner (now the DIFS Director), who may consider the reasonableness of the policy's conditions and exceptions. That is the same statute DIFS cites in Bulletin 2024-26-INS. Rory v Continental Ins Co, 473 Mich 457 (2005).
A Michigan fire insurance policy tries to pay out less than actual cash value on a total loss, citing a policy clause. Is that clause enforceable?

No, not to the extent it undercuts the statutory floor. MCL 500.2833(1)(a) requires the policy to provide, at a minimum, ACV coverage at the time of loss; a clause paying below that floor conflicts with a mandatory statutory provision.

A one-year contractual suit-limitation clause in a Michigan auto policy is clear and unambiguous. The insured argues it's unfair because the claim dragged on. Does Rory let a court strike the clause as unreasonable?

No. Rory holds courts cannot refuse to enforce an unambiguous provision based on a judicial view of reasonableness. The insured's only paths are ambiguity, a statutory tolling rule, or a recognized contract defense.
What year and court decided Rory v Continental Insurance Co, and what was the underlying policy dispute about?
The Michigan Supreme Court, July 28, 2005. The dispute was over a one-year contractual limitation period for suing under an auto policy.
What year and court decided Wilkie v Auto-Owners Insurance Co, overruling reasonable expectations?
The Michigan Supreme Court, July 16, 2003.
What year and court decided Heniser v Frankenmuth Mutual, which set the two step coverage then exclusion analysis and the insured's burden?
The Michigan Supreme Court, July 6, 1995.
What year and court decided Kirschner v Process Design, limiting waiver and estoppel?
The Michigan Supreme Court, May 11, 1999.
What year and court decided Salesin v State Farm, on overhead and profit in ACV payments?
The Michigan Court of Appeals, April 21, 1998, published.
What year and court decided Sunshine Motors v New Hampshire Insurance Co, on anti-concurrent-causation clauses?
The Michigan Court of Appeals, February 22, 1995, published.

An insurer's water exclusion has no "regardless of any other cause or event" language anywhere in it, but a covered peril and an excluded peril both contributed to one loss. Does Sunshine Motors's ACC enforcement automatically defeat the insured's claim?

No. Sunshine Motors enforces ACC language only where it actually appears in the exclusion at issue; without it, that case does not apply. The closest Michigan Supreme Court guidance is Vanguard Ins Co v Clarke, 438 Mich 463 (1991), which refused to let concurrent causation override an unambiguous exclusion in a homeowner's liability policy. No Michigan first-party property holding on a mixed-cause loss without ACC language was opened. Sunshine Motors, 209 Mich App 58 (1995).
A Michigan business claims a virus-related closure caused 'direct physical loss.' Did the Gavrilides court stop at the coverage trigger, or also rule on the insurer's virus exclusion?

Both. Gavrilides first held there was no direct physical loss, then in a separate section held 'defendant properly denied plaintiffs' claim pursuant to the virus exclusion,' rejecting the arguments that the exclusion was vague, against public policy, or limited to physical damage. It also said the ordinance-or-law exclusion 'would appear to' preclude the claim. Gavrilides Mgmt Co v Michigan Ins Co, COA No. 354418 (2022).
Put Heniser's burden-shifting framework in the correct two-step order.

Step 1: the insured must show the loss falls within the coverage grant. Heniser v Frankenmuth Mut Ins Co, 449 Mich 155 (1995). Step 2: only then must the insurer prove an exclusion negates that coverage. Hunt v Drielick, 496 Mich 366 (2014), quoting Fresard v Mich Millers Mut Ins Co, 414 Mich 686, 694 (1982).

A carrier tells a Michigan insured, "reasonable minds could read this policy to cover your loss, so we'll just deny it since our reading is more reasonable." Under Rory and Klapp together, is that a valid way to resolve the dispute?

No. Rory requires unambiguous language to be enforced as written with no judicial reasonableness override, and if the language is genuinely ambiguous, Klapp requires extrinsic evidence to be considered before any "reasonable reading" wins by default.
What did Kirschner v Process Design actually hold on its facts?

The insurer (GAI) was not estopped from enforcing its policy exclusions against the injured plaintiffs in their garnishment action. GAI had sent its insured, Process Design, reservation-of-rights letters, so it satisfied its duty to notify the insured; Michigan law imposes no additional duty on a non-party insurer to notify the plaintiff. Kirschner v Process Design Assocs, 459 Mich 587 (1999).
On an open-peril ('special form') property policy, what is the covered cause of loss, as shown by the commercial form in Gavrilides?

Risks of direct physical loss. The Gavrilides policy's 'Covered Causes of Loss' included 'Risks of Direct Physical Loss,' with the exclusions (for example the ordinance-or-law exclusion in Section B(1)(a)(1) of the 'special form') carving coverage back out. That is the open-peril structure: everything physical is in unless excluded, but the loss must still be direct and physical. Gavrilides Mgmt Co v Michigan Ins Co, COA No. 354418 (2022).
